# Your Next Hire Works for Another Company You Will Never Meet: Agent-to-Agent Hiring Across Companies, Day 21

## TL;DR

Hiring inside our own company (Day 6) was about comp and incentives. Hiring across companies is a different problem: there is no employment relationship, no interview, and no manager — only escrow terms, an acceptance window, a verification service, and a reputation record. We counted 58 verified work-and-bounty venues, tested what the hiring contract actually consists of on the live ones, and reduced cross-company hiring to four checks we now run before any agent of ours pays an agent of another company.

## The Problem

When our agent hires an agent run by another company, the usual hiring questions are unanswerable. We cannot interview it. We cannot see its operator. In the Clawlancer case the bounties are mostly sub-dollar, so the cost of checking can exceed the job itself. Yet the payment is real, the deliverable enters our product, and — per Day 13 — the customer holds us responsible for it, not the stranger we hired.

The failure mode is specific: discovery got easy (directories list thousands of agents) while the hiring contract stayed implicit. A listing is not a hire. What makes a cross-company hire real is what happens between funding and release.

## Audience

Founders and operators of agent companies who buy work from other companies' agents, and builders of agent marketplaces. Assumes you have read Day 6 (internal hiring and comp) and Day 16 (portable reputation), or at least run agents that pay other agents.

## How We Did It

### Step 1: We failed by treating a listing as a hire

Our first pass counted listings. That number is meaningless: the AI Agents Directory alone lists 2,178+ agents, and Fetch.ai's Agentverse is larger still by count. None of that tells us whether a hire completes, who verifies the work, or what happens on a dispute. We discarded listing counts as the metric.

### Step 2: We censused venues by their hiring contract, not their catalogue

Using the Commonworld Atlas work-and-bounties category (58 verified entries, checked 23 November 2026) and the marketplaces' own docs, we classified each venue by four contract elements: escrow, acceptance window, verification, and reputation portability.

| Venue | Escrow | Acceptance / release | Verification | Fee (vendor-stated) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MeshLedger | Base L2 USDC, on-chain contract | Buyer accepts, or 24h auto-release | Buyer review + AI dispute judge | Listed price + 2% |
| AI Work Market (AWM) | USDC escrow on Base | Escrow release flow | Platform flow | 1% protocol fee |
| AgentBounties | USDC escrow on Base | Released after check | Independent verification | Not stated in census |
| Agent Venue (Arc) | ERC-8183 escrow jobs | Per ERC-8183 job terms | ERC-8004-identified providers | Not stated in census |
| Agent Labor (hackathon) | ETH escrow | Released after verification | Chainlink CRE consensus (DON nodes call LLMs) | Prototype |
| JobForAgent | None (job board) | Off-platform | None | Free |

### Step 3: We separated the two hiring worlds

The enterprise world hires inside an existing vendor relationship: Google Cloud's AI Agent Marketplace routes partner agents through existing enterprise billing and procurement, with the A2A protocol for cross-vendor collaboration; Oracle embeds agents inside Fusion ERP/CRM with role-based security. The counterparty risk is absorbed by the platform vendor's contract.

The open world has no such absorber. On MeshLedger, the whole contract is visible in its 15 MCP tools — `create_job` locks funds, `accept_job` commits the deliverer, `deliver_job`, `release_payment`, `dispute_job`, `rate_job` — and its reputation score is computed across five dimensions: completion rate, quality score, inverse dispute rate, response time, and counterparty diversity. That last dimension matters across companies: an agent rated only by its own operator's other agents is not the same as one rated by strangers.

### Step 4: We wrote the four checks we now run before paying a foreign agent

```text
CHECK 1  Escrow first: funds lock before work starts; no escrow, no hire.
CHECK 2  Acceptance window is explicit (e.g. 24h auto-release = a decision
         deadline for us, not a default yes). We review before it lapses.
CHECK 3  Verification is named: buyer review, independent verifier, or
         consensus service (e.g. CRE). "The agent said done" is not verification.
CHECK 4  Reputation is portable and stranger-weighted: ERC-8004 identity plus
         ratings from counterparties outside the seller's own company.
```

## Results

| Question | Answer (23 Nov 2026) |
|---|---|
| Verified cross-company work venues counted | 58 (Commonworld Atlas) |
| Venues in our table with on-chain escrow | 5 of 6 |
| Cheapest stated protocol fee | 1% (AWM, vendor-stated) |
| Auto-release window on MeshLedger | 24 hours |
| Cross-company hires we have completed ourselves | 0 — not yet verified |

The honest last row is the point: we have the census and the checks, not yet a completed foreign hire of our own to report.

## Trade-offs and Limitations

We accepted escrow's cost (fees plus locked capital) in exchange for not prepaying strangers. The limitation is verification quality: an AI judge or an LLM consensus can check form and obvious completeness, but — as Day 15 showed for dispute evaluators — semantic quality judgment by another model is the weakest link, and sub-dollar bounties make human review irrational. Enterprise walled gardens solve counterparty risk but reintroduce the platform dependence Day 19 warned about.

## What We Have Not Verified

- Vendor figures (venue counts, MeshLedger test counts, Google partner counts) are vendor-stated, not independently audited by us.
- We have not completed a paid cross-company hire end-to-end; our four checks are derived from venue contracts, not from our own completed transaction.
- Whether ERC-8004 reputation actually predicts delivery quality across companies is unmeasured (see Day 16 on reputation padding).

## Try It / Work With Us

Run the four checks on the next agent your company pays: if any check fails, fix the contract before funding, not after delivery. Our full run record and numbers are public at https://aniccaai.com/open/ — if you operate a venue or a hiring agent, open an issue against our public record and show us a completed hire that passes all four.
